title: 1945 Australian National Airways Stinson crash
summary: The Stinson Model A aircraft departed Melbourne on a scheduled service to Broken Hill. During the climb approximately 20 minutes after takeoff, a fatigue crack in the main spar of the left wing caused the outer wing to separate, leading to loss of control and a fatal crash near Redesdale. All ten occupants were killed. The investigation established this as the first fatal aircraft accident directly attributed to metal fatigue.
probable_cause: A fatigue crack in the main spar of the left wing caused the outer part of the left wing to separate from the aircraft, resulting in loss of control and fatal impact with terrain.

factors.evidence: fatigue crack had initiated in weld metal on the inner surface of the socket of the main spar lower boom attachment and propagated through the weld metal during many flights
the fatigue crack affected 45% of the cross-section before the lower boom failed, indicating the defect was not detected during inspections
the lower boom failed and the wing folded upward under air loads, causing the outer part of the left wing to separate from the aircraft
the tail assembly also broke free and the aircraft spiralled downward and struck the ground

events.text: Aircraft departed from Melbourne's Essendon Airport at 7:55 am with two pilots and eight passengers bound for Broken Hill via Kerang and Mildura
Aircraft approaching Redesdale, flying at approximately 1000 feet above ground level, 20 minutes after takeoff with strong and gusting south-west wind
Several witnesses heard a sharp crack followed by cessation of engine noise and observed the Stinson spiralling downwards
The outer part of the left wing, outboard of the engine nacelle, separated from the aircraft and drifted slowly to the ground
The entire tail assembly broke free from the fuselage
The wreckage struck the ground inverted and was immediately consumed by fire

title: American Airlines 009
summary: A Douglas DC-3 crashed into wooded terrain on Glade Mountain while descending through rain and clouds on the Washington-Nashville leg of a night flight. The aircraft impacted at 3,910 feet altitude while cruising at 4,000 feet according to the last radio report. Investigation determined the probable cause was the pilot's failure to maintain safe altitude under instrument conditions combined with the company's lax flight dispatch and supervision.
probable_cause: The pilot's failure to properly plan the flight and remain at a safe instrument altitude under existing conditions of bad weather. The company's laxity in dispatching and supervising the flight contributed to the accident.

title: USAAF Boeing B-17 crash on North Barrule
summary: A USAAF B-17G carrying 29 personnel and 2 pilots departed RAF Ridgewell for RAF Nutts Corner. At 10:15 the aircraft was off the northeast coast of the Isle of Man flying at 500 feet altitude. Five minutes later at 10:20, the aircraft flew into the east side of North Barrule, a 1842-foot hill, and exploded in a fireball. All 31 occupants were killed in what became the deadliest aviation accident in the Isle of Man.

title: 1945 New Guinea Gremlin Special rescue
summary: A Douglas C-47 Skytrain on a sightseeing flight over the Baliem Valley interior of New Guinea flew into the side of a mountain. Five passengers survived the initial crash but two, Sergeant Laura Besley and Private Eleanor Hanna, died from injuries the next day. Three survivors were spotted during an air search and evacuated via parachute-dropped paratroopers and then towed by glider over two weeks of rescue operations.

title: Eastern Air Lines 45
summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 45 operating a Douglas DC-3 had a mid-air collision with a USAAF A-26C-35-DT Invader bomber on July 12 1945 at approximately 3100 feet 11.9 miles WNW of Florence South Carolina over Lamar. The A-26 vertical fin struck the port wing of the airliner displacing the engine of the DC-3 which then cut into the fuselage. The DC-3 pilot belly-landed in a cornfield after a 20-to-30-second descent. One airline passenger and two bomber crew members were killed.

title: 1945 Empire State Building B-25 crash
summary: On 28 July 1945, a B-25 Mitchell bomber of the United States Army Air Forces under command of Lieutenant Colonel William Franklin Smith Jr. was conducting a routine personnel transport mission from Bedford Army Air Field in Massachusetts to Newark Metropolitan Airport. Unable to land at LaGuardia due to thick fog, the aircraft became disoriented and turned right instead of left after flying near the Chrysler Building, crashing into the north side of the Empire State Building at 9:40 a.m. between the 78th and 80th floors. The impact killed fourteen people including three crew and eleven civilians, with approximately 20 to 24 others injured.

title: National Airlines 16

location.name: Lake Parker adjacent to Lakeland airport

summary: National Airlines Flight 16, a Lockheed Lodestar, was on its final approach leg to Lakeland, Florida on 5 October 1945. At 12:58 a.m. during approach with seven miles visibility, the pilots established a straight-in descent to runway 09. At 600 feet, the aircraft abruptly entered unexpected cloud and the captain initiated a go-around by retracting the landing gear. However, the aircraft continued low over the runway at approximately 30 feet, passed the runway end, and struck Lake Parker about 1,000 feet beyond. The aircraft skipped another 1,000 feet across the water and sank in 10 feet of water. Two passengers drowned; other occupants were rescued.
probable_cause: The captain's unfamiliarity with the aircraft specifications caused him to wait too long to commit himself to the go-around procedure. The aircraft had no malfunction or failure; the cause was pilot error in timing the escape maneuver.

factors.evidence: the captain's unfamiliarity with the aircraft specifications led him to wait too long to commit to the go-around procedure

The first officer had 5247 hours and 409 hours on the Lodestar but did not prevent the error
aircraft struck the surface of Lake Parker adjacent to the Lakeland airport approximately 1000 ft beyond the end of the runway

events.text: At seven miles from the airfield, the pilots established a straight-in descent to the northeastern runway with visibility of nine miles and scattered clouds at 500 feet.

title: Flight 19
summary: Flight 19 was a group of five Grumman TBF Avenger torpedo bombers that disappeared over the Bermuda Triangle on December 5, 1945, after losing contact during a navigation training flight from Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale. Flight leader Lt. Charles C. Taylor mistook small islands offshore for the Florida Keys after his compasses stopped working, resulting in the flight heading over open sea and away from land. All 14 naval aviators and 13 crew from a search aircraft were lost.
